newsitem.title: USA: CBOT traders say USDA data bullish December corn.
newsitem.headline: CBOT traders say USDA data bullish December corn.

text.p: CBOT traders said USDA's acreage data were bullish for new-crop December corn futures which was called to open two to four cents a bushel higher.
It was also bearish for new-crop November soybean futures, which were forecast to open down eight to 10 cents.
Quarterly stocks data were, however, bullish for old-crop July soybean futures and active bull spreading was expected. July soybeans were called up three to 10 cents.
Stocks data were seen neutral to slightly bearish for old-crop July corn, which was called one to two cents lower.
Wheat futures were seen opening one to three cents a bushel lower with bearish spring wheat acreage data partially offset by mildly constructive quarterly stocks data.
USDA put this year's corn acreage at 80.2 million acres, below its March estimate of 81.4 million and an average forecast in a Reuter survey of analysts of 81.8 million.
Soybean area was higher than expected at 70.9 million acres, up from USDA's March estimate of 68.8 million and an average analyst projection of 68.4 million.
"It's bullish for December corn and bearish for November beans," said Steve Bruce of E.D. and F. Man International.
Old-crop soybeans were, however, seen supported by USDA putting stocks, as of June 1, at 499 million bushels, down from an average analyst projection of 516 million.
"It confirms they overestimated last year's (soybean) crop," a trader said.
Corn stocks at 2.495 billion bushels were slightly higher than an average analyst projection of 2.478 billion.

"The nearby soybeans, with stocks as low as they are, should be friendly, but the acreage estimate as high it is won't be friendly. We'll see a lot of bull spreading," said Jack Scoville, grain analyst with The Price Group.
"In the corn, we'll see the reverse (bear spreading)," Scoville said.
USDA put spring wheat planted area at 19.2 million acres, up from an average analyst projection of 18.1 million and a USDA March estimate of 17.8 million.
Losses in wheat were, however, seen limited by lower than expected stocks, as of June 1, of 444 million bushels, down from an average analyst estimate of 466 million.
